{
{
  "hypotheses": [
    {
      "hypothesis_id": "H1",
      "hypothesis": "Subject-level variation in wearable stress-detection uncertainty is driven by individual differences in baseline autonomic tone, specifically resting heart rate variability (HRV), which influences algorithm calibration accuracy.",
      "proposed_mechanism": "Higher resting HRV improves the calibration of the stress detection algorithm, reducing predictive uncertainty.",
      "causal_path": "Baseline HRV → algorithm calibration accuracy → stress-detection uncertainty",
      "mechanism_variables": [
        "baseline_HRV_ms2",
        "calibration_error_unitless",
        "uncertainty_score"
      ],
      "possible_confounders": [
        "age",
        "fitness_level_VO2max",
        "beta_blocker_use"
      ],
      "control_variables": [
        "age",
        "VO2max_ml_kg_min",
        "beta_blocker_binary"
      ],
      "rival_explanation": "Variation in uncertainty is primarily due to inconsistencies in sensor placement across subjects.",
      "rival_prediction": "Subjects with poorer placement consistency will show higher uncertainty regardless of their baseline HRV.",
      "distinguishing_test": "After statistically controlling for placement variability (e.g., using accelerometer-derived placement metrics), baseline HRV remains a significant predictor of uncertainty.",
      "effect_size_expectation": "medium",
      "effect_size_rationale": "Prior studies report moderate correlations (r≈0.3) between resting HRV and stress classification performance.",
      "minimum_data_needed": [
        "baseline_HRV_recording",
        "placement_consistency_metric",
        "uncertainty_per_subject",
        "age",
        "VO2max_measurement",
        "beta_blocker_status"
      ],
      "testable_prediction": "Subjects with higher baseline HRV will exhibit lower uncertainty scores (negative association).",
      "failure_condition": "No significant negative association between baseline HRV and uncertainty after adjusting for age, VO2max, and beta‑blocker use.",
      "statistical_test_plan": "Linear mixed‑effects model with uncertainty as the outcome, baseline HRV as a fixed effect, random intercept for subject, and age, VO2max, beta‑blocker use as covariates.",
      "falsification_test": "Induce a transient change in resting HRV via paced breathing while holding placement constant; if uncertainty does not change in the predicted direction, the mechanism is falsified."
    },
    {
      "hypothesis_id": "H2",
      "hypothesis": "Individual differences in skin impedance affect PPG signal quality, leading to subject‑level variation in stress‑detection uncertainty.",
      "proposed_mechanism": "Higher skin impedance reduces PPG signal‑to‑noise ratio, which increases the uncertainty of the stress detection model.",
      "causal_path": "skin_impedance → PPG_SNR → stress‑detection uncertainty",
      "mechanism_variables": [
        "skin_impedance_kOhm",
        "PPG_SNR_dB",
        "uncertainty_score"
      ],
      "possible_confounders": [
        "sweat_rate",
        "motion_artifact_level",
        "ambient_temperature"
      ],
      "control_variables": [
        "sweat_rate_mg_cm2_min",
        "accelerometer_variance_g2",
        "ambient_temp_C"
      ],
      "rival_explanation": "Uncertainty differences are mainly caused by non‑individualized algorithm threshold settings.",
      "rival_prediction": "If thresholds are individualized per subject, skin impedance will no longer predict uncertainty.",
      "distinguishing_test": "Compare uncertainty before and after applying individualized thresholds; a persistent effect of skin impedance after threshold adjustment supports the mechanism.",
      "effect_size_expectation": "large",
      "effect_size_rationale": "Skin impedance can vary by >10 kΩ across individuals, producing >10 dB changes in PPG SNR, which prior work links to large shifts in detection error.",
      "minimum_data_needed": [
        "skin_impedance_measurement",
        "PPG_SNR_estimate",
        "uncertainty_per_subject",
        "sweat_rate",
        "accelerometer_variance",
        "ambient_temperature"
      ],
      "testable_prediction": "Higher skin impedance predicts higher uncertainty (positive association).",
      "failure_condition": "No significant positive association between skin impedance and uncertainty after controlling for sweat, motion, and temperature.",
      "statistical_test_plan": "Multiple regression of uncertainty on skin impedance with sweat rate, accelerometer variance, and ambient temperature as covariates.",
      "falsification_test": "Temporarily lower skin impedance using a conductive gel; if uncertainty does not decrease accordingly, the mechanism is falsified."
    },
    {
      "hypothesis_id": "H3",
      "hypothesis": "Variability in the latency of the cortisol stress response creates misalignment between self‑report stress labels and wearable physiological signals, increasing uncertainty.",
      "proposed_mechanism": "Slower cortisol peaks cause temporal mismatch between label timestamps and model‑expected stress signatures, raising uncertainty.",
      "causal_path": "cortisol_response_latency → label_signal_misalignment → stress‑detection uncertainty",
      "mechanism_variables": [
        "cortisol_latency_min",
        "misalignment_score_crosscorr_lag",
        "uncertainty_score"
      ],
      "possible_confounders": [
        "circadian_time",
        "food_intake",
        "stressor_type"
      ],
      "control_variables": [
        "time_of_day_h",
        "fasting_state_binary",
        "stressor_modality_categorical"
      ],
      "rival_explanation": "Uncertainty stems mainly from inconsistent self‑report compliance rather than hormonal timing.",
      "rival_prediction": "Subjects with low compliance will show high uncertainty irrespective of cortisol latency.",
      "distinguishing_test": "After adjusting for self‑report compliance scores, cortisol latency remains a significant predictor of uncertainty.",
      "effect_size_expectation": "medium",
      "effect_size_rationale": "Earlier work shows moderate correlations (r≈0.35) between hormonal response latency and self‑report physiological alignment.",
      "minimum_data_needed": [
        "salivary_cortisol_time_series",
        "self_report_stress_timestamps",
        "uncertainty_per_subject",
        "compliance_score",
        "time_of_day",
        "fasting_state",
        "stressor_type"
      ],
      "testable_prediction": "Longer cortisol latency predicts higher uncertainty (positive association).",
      "failure_condition": "No significant positive association between cortisol latency and uncertainty after controlling for compliance, time of day, fasting, and stressor type.",
      "statistical_test_plan": "Linear mixed‑effects model with uncertainty as outcome, cortisol latency as fixed effect, random subject intercept, and compliance, time of day, fasting, stressor type as covariates.",
      "falsification_test": "Administer a CRH agonist to advance cortisol response; if uncertainty does not decrease as predicted, the mechanism is falsified."
    },
    {
      "hypothesis_id": "H4",
      "hypothesis": "Individual circadian phase influences baseline drift of electrodermal activity (EDA), producing time‑of‑day dependent variation in stress‑detection uncertainty.",
      "proposed_mechanism": "Circadian‑dependent EDA baseline drift alters the background against which stress‑related changes are detected, increasing uncertainty when drift is large.",
      "causal_path": "circadian_phase → EDA_baseline_drift → stress‑detection uncertainty",
      "mechanism_variables": [
        "circadian_phase_h_from_DLMO",
        "EDA_baseline_drift_uS_per_h",
        "uncertainty_score"
      ],
      "possible_confounders": [
        "sleep_deprivation",
        "caffeine_intake",
        "activity_level"
      ],
      "control_variables": [
        "prior_sleep_hours",
        "caffeine_mg",
        "accelerometer_variance_g2"
      ],
      "rival_explanation": "Uncertainty fluctuations are driven primarily by battery voltage decline over the recording session.",
      "rival_prediction": "Lower battery voltage predicts higher uncertainty independent of circadian phase.",
      "distinguishing_test": "After statistically controlling for battery level, circadian phase still predicts uncertainty.",
      "effect_size_expectation": "small",
      "effect_size_rationale": "Prior work shows modest but significant circadian modulation of EDA baseline (≈5‑10 % amplitude).",
      "minimum_data_needed": [
        "circadian_phase_estimate",
        "EDA_baseline_drift",
        "uncertainty_per_subject",
        "battery_voltage",
        "prior_sleep_hours",
        "caffeine_mg",
        "accelerometer_variance"
      ],
      "testable_prediction": "Uncertainty is higher during the biological night (circadian phase 0‑6 h) for individuals with delayed phase.",
      "failure_condition": "No significant interaction between circadian phase and uncertainty after adjusting for battery, sleep, caffeine, and activity.",
      "statistical_test_plan": "Linear mixed‑effects model with uncertainty as outcome, circadian phase, battery level, and their interaction as fixed effects, random intercept for subject, and sleep, caffeine, activity as covariates.",
      "falsification_test": "Conduct a constant‑routine protocol to eliminate circadian variation; if uncertainty still varies with clock time, the mechanism is falsified."
    },
    {
      "hypothesis_id": "H5",
      "hypothesis": "Individual differences in alexithymia increase noise in self‑report stress labels, which propagates to higher model uncertainty.",
      "proposed_mechanism": "Greater alexithymia reduces the reliability of subjective stress reports, inflating label noise and thus the uncertainty of the learned stress detector.",
      "causal_path": "alexithymia_score → label_noise → stress‑detection uncertainty",
      "mechanism_variables": [
        "alexithymia_TAS_score",
        "label_noise_entropy",
        "uncertainty_score"
      ],
      "possible_confounders": [
        "education_level",
        "language_proficiency",
        "mood_disorder_status"
      ],
      "control_variables": [
        "years_education",
        "TOEFL_score",
        "PHQ_9_depression_score"
      ],
      "rival_explanation": "Uncertainty differences arise mainly from variations in stressor intensity across subjects.",
      "rival_prediction": "Higher variability in administered stressor intensity leads to higher uncertainty regardless of alexithymia.",
      "distinguishing_test": "After controlling for stressor‑intensity variance, alexithymia remains a significant predictor of uncertainty.",
      "effect_size_expectation": "medium",
      "effect_size_rationale": "Studies report moderate associations (r≈0.3) between alexithymia and self‑report reliability.",
      "minimum_data_needed": [
        "alexithymia_score",
        "multiple_self_reports_per_stressor_to_compute_label_noise",
        "uncertainty_per_subject",
        "years_education",
        "TOEFL_score",
        "PHQ_9_score",
        "stressor_intensity_variance"
      ],
      "testable_prediction": "Higher alexithymia predicts higher uncertainty (positive association).",
      "failure_condition": "No significant positive association between alexithymia and uncertainty after adjusting for education, language proficiency, and mood disorder.",
      "statistical_test_plan": "Regression of uncertainty on alexithymia with years of education, TOEFL score, and PHQ‑9 as covariates.",
      "falsification_test": "Replace self‑report labels with objective biomarker labels (e.g., cortisol) and retrain the model; if uncertainty no longer correlates with alexithymia, the mechanism is supported; if the correlation persists, it is falsified."
    },
    {
      "hypothesis_id": "H6",
      "hypothesis": "Unmodeled hypertensive subpopulations produce heteroscedastic uncertainty because altered vascular tone changes PPG amplitude and degrades model fit for those subjects.",
      "proposed_mechanism": "Hypertension‑related vascular tone shifts reduce PPG pulse amplitude, increasing model residuals and thus uncertainty for hypertensive individuals.",
      "causal_path": "hypertension_status → PPG_amplitude_shift → model_residual_variance → stress‑detection uncertainty",
      "mechanism_variables": [
        "hypertension_binary",
        "PPG_amplitude_normalized",
        "residual_variance",
        "uncertainty_score"
      ],
      "possible_confounders": [
        "antihypertensive_medication",
        "arterial_stiffness",
        "age"
      ],
      "control_variables": [
        "medication_use_binary",
        "pulse_wave_velocity_m_s",
        "age_years"
      ],
      "rival_explanation": "Uncertainty differences are primarily due to differing physical activity levels between hypertensive and normotensive subjects.",
      "rival_prediction": "After adjusting for activity, hypertension status no longer predicts uncertainty.",
      "distinguishing_test": "Include physical activity as a covariate; if hypertension remains a significant predictor, the mechanism is supported.",
      "effect_size_expectation": "unknown",
      "effect_size_rationale": "No prior work has quantified the uncertainty gap between hypertensive and normotensive wearables; variance‑components analysis is needed.",
      "minimum_data_needed": [
        "hypertension_status",
        "PPG_amplitude",
        "model_residuals_per_window",
        "uncertainty_per_subject",
        "antihypertensive_medication",
        "pulse_wave_velocity",
        "age",
        "physical_activity_counts"
      ],
      "testable_prediction": "Hypertensive subjects exhibit higher uncertainty than normotensive subjects (positive direction).",
      "failure_condition": "No significant difference in uncertainty between hypertensive and normotensive groups after controlling for medication, arterial stiffness, age, and activity.",
      "statistical_test_plan": "Linear mixed‑effects model with uncertainty as outcome, hypertension as fixed effect, random subject intercept, and medication, pulse wave velocity, age, activity as covariates.",
      "falsification_test": "Train separate stress‑detection models for hypertensive and normotensive subsamples; if the uncertainty gap disappears when models are group‑specific, the mechanism is supported; if the gap persists, it is falsified."
    },
    {
      "hypothesis_id": "H7",
      "hypothesis": "Subjects whose feature vectors lie far from the training distribution incur higher model‑based uncertainty due to extrapolation.",
      "proposed_mechanism": "Greater Mahalanobis distance from the training feature distribution signals out‑of‑domain inputs, which Bayesian or ensemble models interpret as higher predictive uncertainty.",
      "causal_path": "Mahalanobis_distance_to_train → predictive_uncertainty",
      "mechanism_variables": [
        "Mahalanobis_distance_unitless",
        "predictive_uncertainty_entropy_or_variance"
      ],
      "possible_confounders": [
        "feature_scaling_method",
        "missing_data_imputation_strategy"
      ],
      "control_variables": [
        "scaling_technique_categorical",
        "imputation_approach_categorical"
      ],
      "rival_explanation": "Uncertainty differences arise mainly from disagreement among ensemble members unrelated to input distance.",
      "rival_prediction": "High ensemble variance can occur even for in‑distribution points, producing uncertainty unrelated to Mahalanobis distance.",
      "distinguishing_test": "After accounting for ensemble variance, Mahalanobis distance still predicts uncertainty.",
      "effect_size_expectation": "large",
      "effect_size_rationale": "Out‑of‑distribution samples routinely increase predictive uncertainty by factors of 2 or more in deep ensembles.",
